chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from his father, from Al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Al-Halabi, from Ibn Muskan, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

I saw as if I were on top of a mountain, and the people were climbing up to it from every side. When they became numerous upon it, it extended with them into the sky. The people began to fall from it from every side until no one remained among them except a small group. This was done five times; in each of those times, the people fell from it and that small group remained. Indeed, Qays ibn Abdullah ibn Ajlan was in that group. He said: He did not remain after that except for about five (days) until he perished.

key_terms.قَيْسُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Qays ibn Abdullah, a specific companion mentioned in the narration

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of the vision of the mountain and the falling people in the hadith of Qays ibn Abdullah?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the concept of *al-Baqiyyah* (the surviving remnant) through a visionary metaphor, where repeated trials cause the masses to fall away, leaving only a faithful few. It specifically identifies Qays ibn Abdullah ibn Ajlan as part of this enduring group, linking the spiritual resilience of the righteous to historical continuity in Shia tradition. The narrative underscores the transient nature of worldly followership versus the permanence of true devotion.
